title: The Shepard tone
hook: A sound that rises forever and never gets any higher.
peek: An audio illusion from Bell Labs in 1964: a tone that seems to climb a staircase with no top. Loop it and your brain insists the pitch keeps going up, while the waveform goes nowhere at all.
lede: In 1964, Roger Shepard, a psychologist at Bell Labs, built a sound that seems to climb a staircase with no top. Play it on a loop and your brain insists the pitch keeps going up. Look at the waveform and nothing is going anywhere at all.

bullets.opening: Octaves that fade in and out
bullets.text: The trick stacks several tones an octave apart. As they climb, the top one fades out and a new low one fades in, so something is always rising and nothing ever arrives.

The psychologist Diana Deutsch found that when two Shepard tones are played half an octave apart, some people hear them rise while others hear them fall. Which one you hear seems to track the speech you grew up around.
In the 1996 game, the endless staircase to Bowser plays a Shepard tone while you climb steps that never seem to end, until you have collected 70 stars.

Zimmer leans on the effect so the tension in Christopher Nolan's 2017 film never lets up. Nolan has said he shaped the script around the same idea, braiding together three stories so the pressure keeps rising.
